EMAIL US: contact@midwest-safety.com

MERCH: Midwest-Safety.com

BE NICE:
The individuals presented in these videos may be suffering from the effects of alcohol, drug abuse, a mental health disorder or simply having a bad day. The videos should NOT be presumed to be representative of their general behavior. Everyone deserves to be treated with respect. 

RIGHT TO BE FORGOTTEN:
Midwest Safety practices the "Right to be Forgotten." If you were the suspect in a lower-level offense, you may email our board to request removal. 
Email: contact@midwest-safety.com

After the interrogation, Anthony was taken to the hospital to be medically cleared and then brought
to jail.
He was held on a $1 million bond and was charged with one count of second degree intentional
murder, not premeditated, and one count of second degree unintentional murder, while committing
a felony.
That underlying felony being assault with a dangerous weapon.
During court, he faced a potential lesser charge of second degree manslaughter,
if the criteria for unintentional murder.
unintentional murder could not be met. Anthony pled not guilty to all charges, leading to a jury
trial focused on the topics of intent and self-defense. The court must answer, if Anthony was
acting reasonably or maliciously. The case was so difficult to determine that a mistrial was declared
after jurors could not come to a unanimous decision, resulting in a new trial. Notably,
this case took place in the Twin Cities just weeks before the murder of George Floyd. As a result,
the case became part of a broader public focus on racial injustice. In the year, the court
deliberated this case. Roughly one in four Minnesota police officers either left the force or
went on extended leave, and in Minneapolis, the force was reduced from about 900 officers to about
580 today. The high-profile nature of the case means that many were watching closely, as the
second jury reached its verdict. During pretrial, defense argued that 79 recorded jail calls with
Anthony were irrelevant and prejudiced evidence, but the court permitted a snippet from one call
due to its relevancy. The jail call was between Anthony and his father and changed the course
of the whole case. Anthony, just answer me one question. You went back to your car because you didn't
have your gun on you. What'd you go back to your car and get your gun for? I had my gun on me. I thought
that would sound better. I had it on me already. I need to talk to someone. That night, I was so
freaked out of everything that happened. I can give them an exact recollection of exactly what
happened. I had had it on me. Prosecutors argued this evidence showed Anthony was willing to bend the story
to appear less guilty, and the extent to which he would go could not be determined. In the end,
the court acquitted Anthony on second-degree murder with intent and convicted him on second-degree
murder without intent while committing a felony, the alternative lesser charge of manslaughter led to
no adjudication. After his conviction, Douglas' family also successfully sued Anthony for damages
totaling over $7.5 million. Roughly one year after the incident in June 2021, he was sentenced to
12.5 years in prison with 397 days of jail credit. This incident occurred in 2020. However, due to
Minnesota's arduous public records laws, it took us almost half a decade to obtain the body cam.
By the time this video is published, the suspect will only need to serve two more years of his prison
sentence.
